To eclipse something means to make it appear dim, insignificant, or invisible — by being so much bigger, brighter, or better that the other thing simply fades into the background.

Think of it this way: imagine you light a small candle in a dark room. It glows beautifully. Now, someone switches on a powerful floodlight. Suddenly, the candle still exists, but nobody notices it anymore. The floodlight has eclipsed the candle.

The verb works on two levels — one literal, one figurative. Both matter.

1. The Literal Meaning (in astronomy)

When one object in space moves in front of another and blocks its light, we say it eclipses it.

  • The Moon eclipses the Sun when it passes directly between the Sun and the Earth, casting a shadow and blocking sunlight.
  • The Earth eclipses the Moon when it moves between the Sun and the Moon, cutting off the light that makes the Moon glow.

This is the original, physical meaning of the word — one body blocking another's light.

2. The Figurative Meaning (in everyday life — and by far the most common use)

This is where the word truly lives. In everyday language, to eclipse someone or something means:

To surpass it so dramatically that it seems to fade, shrink, or disappear by comparison.

It is not just about being better. It is about being so much better — so much brighter, greater, or more impressive — that the other thing loses its visibility, its glory, or its relevance, just like the Sun disappears during a solar eclipse.
The Feeling Packed Inside the Word

This is the key to really understanding "eclipse." It carries a sense of dramatic contrast and total overshadowing. When something eclipses something else:

  • The thing being eclipsed is not necessarily bad or weak on its own.
  • But next to the thing that eclipses it, it seems small and forgettable.
  • The gap between the two is not minor — it is significant.

This is what separates "eclipse" from a weaker word like "beat." You can beat someone by one point. But when you eclipse someone, you leave them so far behind that the comparison almost feels unfair.

Here are clear examples, moving from simple to more complex, so you can see how the word behaves:

  • "Her performance eclipsed everyone else's in the competition."

She did not just win — she was so outstanding that the other performers looked dim by comparison.

  • "The new smartphone completely eclipsed its predecessor."

The older phone, which was once impressive, now seems outdated and unremarkable next to the new one.

  • "His later achievements eclipsed his early successes."

His early wins were real and good — but they were so outshone by what he did later that nobody talks about them anymore.

  • "The scandal eclipsed all the good work the politician had done."

The scandal was so enormous and attention-grabbing that it made all his past accomplishments invisible in the public eye.

  • "The young player has begun to eclipse her mentor."

The student has grown so talented that she now outshines the very person who taught her.
What Makes "Eclipse" Special Compared to Similar Words

You may know words like surpass, outshine, or overshadow. These are all close cousins. Here is how "eclipse" is distinct:

  • Surpass simply means to go beyond or exceed. It is neutral and factual. (She surpassed the target.)
  • Outshine focuses on being brighter or more impressive in a positive, glowing way.
  • Overshadow is similar to eclipse but often carries a slightly negative, darker tone — like something unwelcome casting a shadow over something good. (His personal tragedy overshadowed his career.)
  • Eclipse is the most powerful and absolute of these. It suggests the most complete kind of overshadowing — where the thing being eclipsed almost ceases to be noticed, just as the Sun disappears in a total eclipse. It works in both positive contexts (a great achievement eclipsing a lesser one) and negative ones (bad news eclipsing good news).
The Subject and Object: Who Eclipses Whom?

The structure of the verb is straightforward:

[The greater thing] eclipses [the lesser thing].

The subject is always the thing doing the overshadowing. The object is the thing being made invisible.

  • ✅ The sequel eclipsed the original film. (The sequel is greater; the original is now in its shadow.)
  • ✅ Her talent eclipsed his. (Her talent is so much greater that his fades next to it.)

To eclipse something is to surpass it so completely — in size, talent, importance, or impact — that it fades into insignificance, just like the Sun disappearing behind the Moon.

Master that image, and you will never misuse this word.
